passages.t: A strong tower, and a wall in the imagination
passages.happening:
‘He who isolates himself pursues selfish desires; he rebels against all sound judgment’ (verse 1). ‘A fool does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions’ (verse 2).

‘The words of a man’s mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a bubbling brook’ (verse 4). Partiality in court is not good (verse 5). A fool's mouth brings him strife and ruin (verses 6-7). ‘The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being’ (verse 8).

Then two refuges side by side. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe” (verse 10). ‘A rich man’s wealth is his fortified city; it is like a high wall in his imagination’ (verse 11). ‘Before his downfall a man’s heart is proud, but humility comes before honor’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is about the places people run for safety. Some retreat into isolation (verse 1), some into their own opinions (verse 2), some into wealth (verse 11), some into many companions who cannot really help (verse 24). Against them all stands one true refuge, the name of the LORD.

Israelite towns had walls strengthened with towers, and some had a fortified tower inside the walls as a last refuge. The name of the LORD is like that: the place the righteous run to when everything else fails.

Verse 11 picks up 10:15, the rich man's fortified city, and adds a barbed phrase: in his imagination. One refuge is real. The other only feels real.

Gossip is pictured as delicacies eaten eagerly and digested deep inside, which is exactly how rumors are taken in and kept. The same saying comes again in 26:22.
passages.later: The psalmist prays the same: ‘For You have been my refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy’ (Psalm 61:3). And the book of Judges tells of a town that ran to its tower: ‘But there was a strong tower inside the city, and all the men, women, and leaders of the city fled there’ (Judges 9:51).
passages.asks: Everyone runs somewhere when trouble comes. Ask where you run first: to your own opinions, your savings, your friends, or the LORD. And ask whether any wall you trust is only high in your imagination.

passages.t: Hearing both sides, and the power of the tongue
passages.happening:
To answer a matter before hearing it is folly and shame (verse 13). “The spirit of a man can endure his sickness, but who can survive a broken spirit?” (verse 14). ‘The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge’ (verse 15). ‘A man’s gift opens doors for him, and brings him before great men’ (verse 16).

‘The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him’ (verse 17). ‘Casting the lot ends quarrels and separates strong opponents’ (verse 18). ‘An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city, and disputes are like the bars of a castle’ (verse 19).

And at the center of the chapter: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Many of these sayings come from the law court at the city gate, where each side stated its case before the elders. Verse 17 is what every judge learned: the first speaker always sounds convincing until the other side questions him. Verse 13 warns judges, and everyone else, against answering before hearing. When the evidence could not decide, the lot settled it fairly (verse 18).

In the ancient world, approaching a king or official usually meant bringing a gift. Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau, and the queen of Sheba brought gifts to Solomon. Such gifts were expected courtesy, different from bribes that bent a judgment, though the line could blur.

Brothers often shared land and inheritance, and a quarrel between them could last for generations, as the stories of Jacob and Esau and of Joseph and his brothers show. That is why an offended brother is harder to win than a walled city.

Verse 14 is honest. A strong spirit can carry a sick body. But a broken spirit is a heavier weight.

If sadness has settled on you and will not lift, these verses do not shame you. When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: The law required judges to ‘investigate thoroughly’ (Deuteronomy 19:18). And the psalm speaks to the broken spirit of verse 14: ‘He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds’ (Psalm 147:3).
passages.asks: Words can give life or death. Ask what your words have been giving to the people closest to you this week. And ask whether you have judged a matter after hearing only one side.

passages.t: A wife, a poor man's plea, and a friend closer than a brother
passages.happening:
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD” (verse 22).

‘The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly’ (verse 23).

‘A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is framed by companionship: the man who isolates himself at the start, and the man of many companions at the end. Neither has what he needs. What he needs is one true friend.

Verse 24 is hard in Hebrew. Its first line may mean that a man of many companions comes to ruin, or that some companions are only for company, and translations differ. The second line is clear: there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.

Verse 23 is an observation, like 14:20. It reports how the rich often speak to the poor. It does not approve of it.
passages.later: The Bible's first word on marriage stands behind verse 22: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper” (Genesis 2:18). And David grieved for a friend closer than a brother: ‘I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother’ (2 Samuel 1:26).
passages.hard:
Verse 22 says he who finds a wife finds a good thing. What about those who are single, or whose marriages are unhappy?

The saying celebrates marriage as a gift from God and a sign of his favor, echoing Genesis 2:18, where it is not good for the man to be alone. But like other proverbs it describes a general truth, not a rule for every case. Proverbs itself is honest that marriage can be miserable. It warns about a quarrelsome home (19:13; 21:9), and it praises a prudent wife as a gift from the LORD precisely because not every marriage is a happy one (19:14). Read as a promise that every marriage will be good, the verse would be false. Read as praise for a good marriage as one of God's great gifts, it is true.

The verse also does not say that being unmarried is a lesser life. Jesus was unmarried, and Paul, also unmarried, spoke of singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 32-35). Christians have long held both marriage and singleness to be honorable callings. The verse invites thanks from those who have found a good spouse. It passes no verdict on those who have not.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.
passages.asks: There is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. Ask whether you have one friend like that, and whether you are that friend to anyone. And if you are married, ask how you could treat your husband or wife this week as the good gift the verse says they are.
